name: Automatically Correcting Large Language Models: Surveying the Landscape of Diverse Automated Correction Strategies
authors: Liangming Pan, Michael Saxon, Wenda Xu, Deepak Nathani, Xinyi Wang, William Yang Wang (University of California, Santa Barbara). arXiv first submission 2023 (2308.03188).
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (TACL), Volume 12, pp. 484-506, MIT Press, 2024. DOI: 10.1162/tacl_a_00660.
code_url: No standalone official code repository (survey). A companion reading list / curated bibliography exists; the paper is tracked in community lists such as dongxiangjue/Awesome-LLM-Self-Improvement and tianyi-lab style self-correction reading lists.
reflection_type: Survey/analysis (not a single method). Taxonomizes the full landscape of automated-feedback correction, spanning verbal-self-critique (self-refine, self-feedback), tool-verified correction (compiler/interpreter/symbolic-solver/retrieval), learned-critic-model approaches (trained reward/critic models, PRM), search-guided generation (beam/tree search with step feedback), and multi-agent-debate. Its own contribution is the conceptual framework, not a new reflection mechanism.
feedback_source: Surveys all sources. Organized into two top-level classes: (1) self-feedback (the LLM itself as critic, e.g. Self-Refine, Reflexion) and (2) external feedback subdivided into other trained models, external tools (code interpreters/compilers, symbolic solvers, BMC), external knowledge sources (Wikipedia/web/retrieval), and external evaluation metrics. Human feedback (RLHF) is covered for completeness but the survey's focus is automated feedback.
iteration_structure: Surveys all of them. Distinguishes single-shot (e.g. one-pass post-edit, re-ranking/generate-then-rank) vs iterative-refine (the 'Iter.' column in Table 2 marks iterative vs non-iterative post-hoc methods, e.g. Self-Refine/Reflexion iterative; SelfCheckGPT/RARR non-iterative) and search-based generation-time correction (stochastic beam search, Tree-of-Thoughts). Reflexion is the episodic-retry-with-reset exemplar surveyed.
reflection_object: Survey covers the full range. Two main targets per the framework's 'Refine Model': (1) the output itself (output content / reasoning chain / code), repaired during or after generation without weight change (generation-time and post-hoc correction); and (2) the model parameters/weights themselves via training-time correction (fine-tuning, self-training, RLHF/RLAIF, model editing). Prompt/context-level correction (e.g. MemPrompt) is also noted. Primary axis 1 of the taxonomy is explicitly 'What gets corrected?' answered at the error-type level: hallucination, unfaithful reasoning, toxic/biased/harmful content, and flawed code.
learning_locus: n/a (analysis/survey). The survey itself performs no weight update; it organizes the literature precisely along this axis, distinguishing training-time correction (gradient_weight_update) from generation-time and post-hoc correction (in_context_verbal, no weight update).
requires_training: n/a for the survey itself. As a taxonomy it explicitly classifies surveyed methods by learning method: ICL (in-context, no training), SL (supervised fine-tuning), and RL (e.g. PPO-based RLHF/RLAIF, CodeRL, RL4F, Reflexion's RL variant). The 'When to correct' dimension separates training-time (parameter update via SFT/RL) from post-hoc (no parameter update).
reward_or_critic_model: Surveys the spectrum. Its 'Critic Model (Doctor)' abstraction C: X x Y -> F covers: self-as-judge (LLM critiques itself), separately trained reward/critic models (RLHF reward models, PRM, DIVERSE, REFINER), verifiable/tool-derived signals (program executors, symbolic solvers, oracle verifiers like ALGO), external evaluation metrics, and external knowledge. Feedback format is taxonomized as scalar-value vs natural-language.
distillation_target: Survey-level. Covers the cases where correction is distilled into model weights (training-time self-training: STaR, Self-Improve, ReST, RLAIF distill correct/positively-evaluated outputs back into the model). Also discusses post-hoc correction collecting frequent-mistake/correction pairs to feed periodic training-time correction (a proposed continual-improvement pipeline), and prompt-level memory (MemPrompt). Episodic memory of past errors is exemplified by the surveyed Reflexion.
emergent_vs_engineered: Predominantly engineered. The surveyed paradigms (Self-Refine, Reflexion, CRITIC, Self-Debug, debate) are prompt/scaffold-engineered correction pipelines built around the Language-Critic-Refine framework. The survey predates reasoning-model RL-emergent self-correction (o1/R1 'aha'); it instead frames the open question of whether self-repair is an emergent ability of certain large models (citing Olausson et al.'s finding that self-repair gains appear mainly with GPT-4-level feedback).
memory_type: Survey-level (not a single memory design). Discusses scratchpad/iterative refinement (within-episode), episodic memory of prior trial errors (Reflexion), prompt-level memory of past feedback (MemPrompt), and weight-based 'memory' via fine-tuning/self-training. Continual/life-long self-improvement with persistent learning is raised as an under-explored future direction.
memory_persistence: Survey-level. Most surveyed methods operate within-episode (single task refinement) or cross-episode within a task (Reflexion-style retry). The survey explicitly flags cross-task/continual (life-long) self-improvement and the associated catastrophic-forgetting risk as open, under-explored problems.
memory_curation_mechanism: n/a (survey does not propose a memory-curation method). It notes, as future work, that post-hoc correction could be used to collect the most-frequent mistakes and their corrections to drive periodic training-time correction (a form of curated retention), and discusses model editing for targeted, side-effect-limited updates.
error_localization_granularity: Surveys multiple granularities. Spans holistic/outcome-level (re-rank or accept/reject whole outputs), response-level (post-hoc revision of full output), and step-level / process-level (process reward models like PRM/Lightman, step-wise reasoning verification, stochastic beam search over intermediate reasoning steps, Tree-of-Thoughts). Code is corrected at block/program level using execution feedback. Multi-agent debate operates at agent-level.
intra_task_vs_inter_task: Both, as a survey. Generation-time and most post-hoc methods are intra-task (refine within a single task instance, e.g. Self-Refine). Reflexion and training-time self-training (STaR, Self-Improve, ReST) carry experience inter-task / across instances. The survey treats this implicitly through its training-time vs generation-time vs post-hoc timing axis rather than as a named dimension.
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: Survey covers all three. Generation-time correction = mid-trajectory recovery (correct/guide errors as generation proceeds, e.g. feedback-guided beam search). Post-hoc correction = post-hoc revision (fix after a full output is produced). Training-time correction = avoidance (fix the model so future generations avoid the error). Reflexion-style retry-with-reset is the episodic-avoidance exemplar.
task_domains: Survey spans: code generation/synthesis, math & reasoning (arithmetic, deductive/proof, commonsense, multi-hop QA), open-domain QA & fact-checking, machine translation (automatic post-editing), summarization, dialogue/response generation, story/open-ended generation, toxicity/harmful-content/detoxification, controlled text generation, planning, and general alignment. Dedicated application sections: factual correction, reasoning tasks, code synthesis, and other (open-ended generation, MT, summarization).
benchmarks: As a survey it does not run benchmarks itself; it aggregates methods evaluated on tasks/datasets such as HumanEval/MBPP-style code generation, GSM8K-style arithmetic reasoning, HotpotQA/multi-hop QA, proof-generation (EntailmentBank-style), machine translation (WMT), summarization, commonsense reasoning, and toxicity (RealToxicityPrompts-style) benchmarks referenced through the surveyed primary works. No single headline benchmark suite is the survey's own.
headline_result: No quantitative headline result of its own (survey). Its primary contributions are: (1) a unifying conceptual framework with three roles — Language Model (patient), Critic Model (doctor/diagnosis), Refine Model (treatment); (2) a five-dimension taxonomy — what gets corrected, source of feedback, format of feedback, when feedback is used, how to correct; and (3) categorization of works into training-time, generation-time, and post-hoc correction (Tables 1-2 catalog ~60 representative methods).
baselines: n/a (survey has no experimental baselines). It positions itself relative to prior surveys: Fernandes et al. (2023) on human feedback for language generation, and broader alignment/continual-learning surveys; its differentiator is the focus on automated (vs human) feedback for self-correction.
gains_vs_baseline: n/a — no experimental gains reported; this is a literature survey/taxonomy, not an empirical method.
compute_cost_profile: Discussed qualitatively rather than measured. The survey notes the practical cost trade-offs of each timing strategy: training-time correction is most fundamental but highest compute (rollouts/gradient steps) and infeasible for giant closed-source LLMs; post-hoc correction is more immediate and less costly but adds inference iterations (extra API calls per refinement loop); generation-time correction adds search/decoding overhead. No numeric multipliers are given.
known_limitations: As stated in Sections 6-7: (1) self-repair is often bottlenecked by feedback quality — Olausson et al. found substantial code self-repair gains only when feedback came from expert humans or GPT-4, raising whether self-correction is an emergent ability of only the largest models; (2) lack of theoretical justification for why self-correction works (tied to calibration/metacognition); (3) no robust quantitative metrics or diagnostic benchmarks to compare self-correction strategies; (4) continual/life-long self-improvement is under-explored and risks catastrophic forgetting; (5) model-editing-based correction lacks generalization and introduces side effects; (6) training-time correction is infeasible for closed-source LLMs and requires 'optimizable' feedback. Scope limit: the survey predates reasoning-model RL-emergent self-correction (o1/R1).
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: Survey-wide, this is a central organizing variable. It explicitly contrasts intrinsic self-feedback against external-tool/verifier, external-knowledge, and oracle signals (e.g. ALGO's oracle verifier, program executors, symbolic solvers). It foregrounds Olausson et al.'s finding that self-repair improvements largely depend on high-quality external feedback (expert humans / GPT-4), and that without good feedback self-correction is limited — anticipating the Kamoi/Huang critique that follows it.
self_correction_efficacy: task-dependent / often requires-strong-feedback. The survey reports broad empirical effectiveness across many tasks but is candid that efficacy hinges on feedback quality and that intrinsic self-correction without external signals is questionable (citing Olausson et al.). Code correction works well because execution feedback is cheap and reliable; reasoning correction is harder because reliable intermediate references are scarce.
calibration_effect: Discussed as theory, not measured. Section 7.1 ties self-correction ability to calibration and metacognitive awareness (Kadavath et al. 2022): pre-trained LMs are reasonably calibrated on self-evaluation in few-shot settings, while RLHF-tuned models need temperature adjustment to recover calibration. The survey treats calibration as an enabling factor for self-correction rather than reporting an empirical improve/degrade outcome.
failure_attribution_capability: classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy). The survey provides a taxonomy of the errors targeted for correction — hallucination, unfaithful reasoning, toxic/biased/harmful content, and flawed code — and organizes corrective strategies against them. It does not attribute failures to specific agents or steps in a multi-agent trace (that is the domain of later attribution work like Who&When/MAST).
failure_mode_addressed: Targets/organizes correction for: hallucination (factual errors, fabricated citations), unfaithful reasoning (conclusion not following the reasoning chain), toxic/biased/harmful generation, and flawed/incorrect code. Relates to MAST-style modes such as superficial/ineffective self-reflection (its discussion of when self-correction fails without good feedback) though it predates the MAST 14-mode taxonomy.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: None. As a survey it releases no dataset, benchmark, or trace corpus; it provides a taxonomy and a curated catalog of ~60 methods (Tables 1-2) rather than a reusable resource. It calls for building diagnostic benchmarks for self-correction as future work.
builds_on: Prior human-feedback survey by Fernandes et al. (2023); foundational methods it organizes including RLHF (Ouyang et al. 2022), Constitutional AI/RLAIF (Bai et al. 2022b), STaR (Zelikman et al. 2022), Self-Improve (Huang et al. 2022), Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), CRITIC (Gou et al. 2023), Self-Debug (Chen et al. 2023d), Tree-of-Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023a), PRM (Lightman et al. 2023), Multiagent Debate (Du et al. 2023), and calibration/metacognition work (Kadavath et al. 2022).
extended_by_or_inspired: Directly succeeded by the critical survey 'When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs' (Kamoi, Saxon, et al., TACL 2024, DOI 10.1162/tacl_a_00713), which shares authorship and sharpens the oracle-feedback-dependency critique; also widely cited as a reference taxonomy in subsequent LLM self-improvement / self-correction reading lists and surveys (e.g. Awesome-LLM-Self-Improvement) and follow-on self-correction methods.
citation_count: ~160 (Semantic Scholar, read from the paper page in 2026; figure is approximate and growing). The Semantic Scholar Graph API could not independently confirm due to rate-limiting at fetch time.
reasoning_model_native: No / predates them. The survey (2023-2024) targets prompt-and-feedback self-correction pipelines for standard LLMs (GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era) and does not cover o1/R1-style models with RL-trained built-in reflection. Its open questions about whether self-correction is an emergent large-model ability foreshadow that line.
on_policy_distillation_link: Indirect. It surveys self-training methods (STaR, Self-Improve, ReST, RLAIF) that retrain a model on its own positively-evaluated/corrected generations — conceptually adjacent to on-policy distillation / self-distillation of correction behavior into weights — but it does not analyze on-policy distillation as such.
sample_efficiency: n/a — not an empirical method; no trials-to-gain numbers. The survey notes that post-hoc iterative refinement adds inference iterations and that training-time correction is costlier in rollouts/gradient steps, but reports no sample-efficiency measurements.
